parts.name: Mk1 Capsule
parts.desc: One seat, basic life support. Cramped but light.
parts.role: The cabin: one seat, the controls, and the air the crew breathes.
parts.detail: The smallest cabin that keeps a person alive: a seat, a window, life support for the trip and the computer that flies the ship. Light and cheap, but nothing spare: every extra bottle of oxygen is a part you add outside.

parts.name: Mk2 Capsule
parts.desc: Roomier cabin, better instruments.
parts.role: The cabin: the crew, the controls and life support, with room to move.
parts.detail: A roomier cabin with better instruments and a little more power. Still the heaviest single piece of hardware on most ships, which is why it sits on top: the rest of the stack is built to carry it.

parts.name: Mk3 Capsule
parts.desc: Big cabin with its own spare oxygen. Heavy.
parts.role: A big cabin with its own spare oxygen. Heavy.
parts.detail: The flagship cabin: more room, more power, a spare oxygen supply built in, and the most reliable systems. The price is mass, and mass is paid in propellant.

parts.name: Pointed nose, small
parts.desc: A slim ogive for a small stack.
parts.role: A slim nose for a small ship.
parts.detail: A small ogive fairing. Less frontal area means less drag in the thick air of the first two minutes, where most of the aerodynamic loss happens.
cons: Small: looks odd on a wide body

parts.name: Pointed nose cone
parts.desc: Low drag through thick air.
parts.role: A sharp nose that cuts through thick air.
parts.detail: The fairing on top of the stack. A pointed nose has the least drag in the thick air of the first minutes of flight, which saves propellant and keeps the aerodynamic load low.

parts.name: Pointed nose, large
parts.desc: A big ogive for a wide stack.
parts.role: A big nose for a wide ship.
parts.detail: A large ogive fairing for the widest bodies. More frontal area than the medium one, but the shape still cuts the air cleanly.
pros: Clean shape for a wide body

parts.name: Blunt nose cone
parts.desc: Cheaper and tougher, more drag.
parts.role: A rounded nose: cheaper, tougher, more drag.
parts.detail: A blunt nose is easier to build and takes a hit better, but pushes more air out of the way. The drag costs a little propellant on the way up.

parts.name: Hammerhead fairing
parts.desc: Wider than the body: room for a bulky payload.
parts.role: A fairing wider than the rocket under it.
parts.detail: A hammerhead fairing is wider than the stage below, so a bulky payload fits inside. Its own skin shields what is under it from one debris strike. The price: more drag, and a wide nose pulls the centre of pressure forward, so put bigger fins low.
pros: Shields the top from one hit
cons: Pulls the centre of pressure forward
parts.real: Atlas V 5 m fairing, Delta II 3 m "hammerhead"

parts.name: Payload attach fitting
parts.desc: The cone that bolts the payload to the stage.
parts.role: The standard interface between the payload and the stage under it.
parts.detail: A truncated cone with a bolted ring at the top and a clamp band at the bottom. It carries the whole payload through launch loads, then lets it go cleanly with push-off springs. Every launcher has a standard one, so a payload built for one rocket fits another.
cons: Mass that does no work after separation

parts.name: Spin table & clamp band
parts.desc: Spins the stage above like a rifle bullet before it fires.
parts.role: A turntable that spins the kick motor and payload for stability, and the band that releases them.
parts.detail: Small solid motors have no steering. The spin table turns the motor and payload to about 50 rpm before they separate, so gyroscopic stiffness keeps them pointed during the burn, like a thrown football. A Marman clamp band holds everything until pyrotechnic bolts cut it. Dawn was spun this way before its Star 48 fired.
parts.real: Delta II spin table and 3712 clamp band

parts.name: Guidance electronics ring
parts.desc: The brain of the launcher: flight computer, gyros, radios.
parts.role: The flight computer, inertial platform and radios that fly the launcher.
parts.detail: A ring of boxes around the top of the stage: the flight computer that runs the guidance program, the inertial measurement unit (gyroscopes and accelerometers) that tells it where the rocket is pointing, the telemetry transmitter, the range-safety receiver and the batteries that run them. With a dedicated guidance section the ship flies more precisely and catches faults the capsule computer would miss: reliability goes up 3 %.

parts.name: Miniskirt & support truss
parts.desc: An open truss: light, and a place to hang the pressure bottles.
parts.role: An open lattice that carries thrust loads and holds the helium and nitrogen spheres.
parts.detail: Where a stage does not need a skin, a truss of struts carries the load with much less mass. The spheres, valves and cables bolt to it, out in the open, where technicians can reach them on the pad. On the Delta II second stage the miniskirt and truss carried the tanks, the engine and the guidance ring.
pros: Hard points for spheres and equipment
cons: No aerodynamic skin: must sit under a fairing or interstage
parts.real: Delta II second-stage miniskirt and support truss

parts.name: Interstage
parts.desc: The hollow ring between two stages, hiding the upper nozzle.
parts.role: The skin that joins two stages and shelters the upper engine bell.
parts.detail: A hollow cylinder of skin and stringers. It joins the stages, protects the upper engine nozzle during ascent, and holds the separation charges and the small retro and settling motors. When the lower stage is done, the interstage goes with it.

parts.name: Centerbody section
parts.desc: The stiff ring between the fuel tank and the oxidizer tank.
parts.role: The structural section between two tanks: where the booster loads come in.
parts.detail: Real stages keep fuel and oxidizer in separate tanks with a short, stiff section between them. The centerbody (intertank) takes the thrust of the strap-on boosters and the bending loads of flight, so neither tank wall has to. Equipment bolts to it without piercing a tank.
pros: Hard points without piercing a tank
parts.real: Delta II centerbody section, Saturn V intertank

parts.name: Kerolox Tank S
parts.desc: 12 m³ of kerosene and liquid oxygen.
parts.role: A small tank of kerosene and liquid oxygen: 12 t of propellant.
parts.detail: Kerosene is dense, so this tank holds a lot of propellant for its size. It feeds kerolox engines only; any other engine treats it as dead weight.
pros: Dense fuel: lots of mass in a small tank
parts.real: Falcon 9 / Atlas RP-1 and LOX tanks

parts.name: Kerolox Tank M
parts.desc: 25 m³ of kerosene and liquid oxygen.
parts.role: A medium tank of kerosene and liquid oxygen: 25 t of propellant.
parts.detail: Kerosene is dense, so this tank holds a lot of propellant for its size. It feeds kerolox engines only; any other engine treats it as dead weight.
pros: Dense fuel: lots of mass in a small tank
Good balance of mass and height
parts.real: Falcon 9 / Atlas RP-1 and LOX tanks

parts.name: Kerolox Tank L
parts.desc: 45 m³ of kerosene and liquid oxygen.
parts.role: The biggest tank of kerosene and liquid oxygen: 45 t of propellant.
parts.detail: Kerosene is dense, so this tank holds a lot of propellant for its size. It feeds kerolox engines only; any other engine treats it as dead weight.
pros: Dense fuel: lots of mass in a small tank
parts.real: Falcon 9 / Atlas RP-1 and LOX tanks

parts.name: Methalox Tank S
parts.desc: 12 m³ of methane and liquid oxygen.
parts.role: A small tank of methane and liquid oxygen: 9.6 t of propellant.
parts.detail: Methane is lighter than kerosene for the same volume, so this tank holds less mass but burns cleaner. Methane can be made on Mars from ice and the air, which matters for the trip home.
parts.real: Starship / New Glenn methane and LOX tanks

parts.name: Methalox Tank M
parts.desc: 25 m³ of methane and liquid oxygen.
parts.role: A medium tank of methane and liquid oxygen: 20 t of propellant.
parts.detail: Methane is lighter than kerosene for the same volume, so this tank holds less mass but burns cleaner. Methane can be made on Mars from ice and the air, which matters for the trip home.
pros: Good balance of mass and height
parts.real: Starship / New Glenn methane and LOX tanks

parts.name: Methalox Tank L
parts.desc: 45 m³ of methane and liquid oxygen.
parts.role: The biggest tank of methane and liquid oxygen: 36 t of propellant.
parts.detail: Methane is lighter than kerosene for the same volume, so this tank holds less mass but burns cleaner. Methane can be made on Mars from ice and the air, which matters for the trip home.
parts.real: Starship / New Glenn methane and LOX tanks

parts.name: Hydrolox Tank S
parts.desc: 12 m³ of hydrogen and liquid oxygen.
parts.role: A small tank of hydrogen and liquid oxygen: 4.2 t of propellant.
parts.detail: Hydrogen is the lightest fuel there is, and the bulkiest: this tank holds little mass for its size, and the insulation that keeps the hydrogen from boiling off weighs more than the tank.
pros: Best Isp with a hydrolox engine
cons: Little mass per tank, boils off during the cruise
parts.real: Shuttle External Tank, Centaur, Delta IV

parts.name: Hydrolox Tank M
parts.desc: 25 m³ of hydrogen and liquid oxygen.
parts.role: A medium tank of hydrogen and liquid oxygen: 8.8 t of propellant.
parts.detail: Hydrogen is the lightest fuel there is, and the bulkiest: this tank holds little mass for its size, and the insulation that keeps the hydrogen from boiling off weighs more than the tank.
pros: Best Isp with a hydrolox engine
Good balance of mass and height
cons: Little mass per tank, boils off during the cruise
parts.real: Shuttle External Tank, Centaur, Delta IV

parts.name: Hydrolox Tank L
parts.desc: 45 m³ of hydrogen and liquid oxygen.
parts.role: The biggest tank of hydrogen and liquid oxygen: 15.8 t of propellant.
parts.detail: Hydrogen is the lightest fuel there is, and the bulkiest: this tank holds little mass for its size, and the insulation that keeps the hydrogen from boiling off weighs more than the tank.
pros: Best Isp with a hydrolox engine
cons: Little mass per tank, boils off during the cruise
parts.real: Shuttle External Tank, Centaur, Delta IV

parts.name: Engine, small pump
parts.desc: 100 kN turbopump. Chamber, nozzle and cycle are yours to choose.
parts.role: A small engine, 100 kN: an upper-stage or lander class.
parts.detail: The small turbopump moves enough propellant for 100 kN of thrust: fine for a tiny ship or an upper stage, not enough to lift a crewed vehicle off the pad. Choose the chamber (fuel), the nozzle, the pump cycle and the igniter.
cons: 100 kN cannot lift a crewed ship

parts.name: Engine, medium pump
parts.desc: 300 kN turbopump. Chamber, nozzle and cycle are yours to choose.
parts.role: A medium engine, 300 kN.
parts.detail: The medium turbopump: 300 kN of thrust and a reasonable price. Lifts about 25 tonnes with a healthy margin. Choose the chamber (fuel), the nozzle, the pump cycle and the igniter.
cons: Lifts about 25 t with margin, no more

parts.name: Engine, large pump
parts.desc: 1,000 kN turbopump. Runs hot at full throttle.
parts.role: A large engine, 1,000 kN. Runs hot at full throttle.
parts.detail: The large turbopump moves almost 300 kg of propellant a second: a megawatt-class machine. It is the engine for a Mars-capable single stage, and it overheats fastest at full throttle.

parts.name: Strap-on solid motor
parts.desc: Thrust augmentation solid: 480 kN off the pad, 63 s, then dead weight.
parts.role: A solid motor clamped to the side: huge thrust at liftoff, for the money.
parts.detail: A steel or composite tube packed with solid propellant (ammonium perchlorate, aluminium powder, rubber binder). Light it and it burns to the end: no throttle, no shutdown. Delta II flew with nine of these. They are the cheapest thrust there is for the first minute, but in this hangar nothing separates in flight, so the empty casing rides along as dead mass. Use ×2 or ×3 symmetry.
cons: Empty casing stays attached (no staging yet)
parts.real: GEM-40 (Delta II): 644 kN, 274 s, 11.8 t propellant

parts.name: Large strap-on solid
parts.desc: 800 kN for 90 s. The Atlas V / Vulcan class strap-on.
parts.role: A bigger solid motor: 800 kN for a heavy stack.
parts.detail: The large graphite-epoxy strap-on. Each one adds 800 kN of thrust and fourteen tonnes of propellant. Two of them lift a stack the main engine alone could never move. The burned-out casing stays attached in this hangar, so each costs Δv later.
cons: Empty casing stays attached (no staging yet)

parts.name: Kick motor, small
parts.desc: A Star-48 class third-stage motor in the stack.
parts.role: A compact solid motor that adds a final push.
parts.detail: The third-stage motor of the Dawn launch: a titanium sphere of solid propellant with a short nozzle, 66 kN for 87 seconds. Spin-stabilised, it needs no guidance of its own. Here it adds its propellant and thrust to the stack.
pros: Two tonnes of propellant in a small package
cons: Isp 286 s: worse than any liquid engine
parts.real: Star 48B: 66 kN, 286 s, 2,011 kg propellant, 126 kg empty

parts.name: Kick motor, medium
parts.desc: A larger spherical solid motor for the stack.
parts.role: A bigger kick motor: 3.3 t of solid propellant.
parts.detail: The larger spherical motor. Solid motors have the best propellant mass fraction of anything in the hangar (the case is 6 % of the mass), but the exhaust is slow: Isp 290 s.
pros: Best mass fraction in the hangar

parts.name: Small fin
parts.desc: A small feather for a small arrow.
parts.role: A small fin: a little stability for little mass.
parts.detail: A short fin for a light stack. Fins pull the centre of pressure to the tail; small fins do it gently. Use ×3 or ×4 symmetry.
cons: Little stability on a tall stack

parts.name: Fin
parts.desc: Moves the centre of pressure back. Use ×3 or ×4 symmetry.
parts.role: A fin: moves the centre of pressure to the tail.
parts.detail: Fins are the feathers on the arrow. Mounted low on the stack they pull the centre of pressure behind the centre of mass, so the ship flies nose-first instead of tumbling. Use ×3 or ×4 symmetry.
pros: Pulls the centre of pressure back

parts.name: Large fin
parts.desc: Bigger feathers for a taller arrow.
parts.role: A big fin for a tall stack.
parts.detail: A larger fin for a longer vehicle. More side area low down means more stability in thick air, at the cost of a little mass and drag.
pros: More stability for a tall stack

parts.name: Wiring tunnel
parts.desc: The raceway that carries cables and lines down the outside of the tank.
parts.role: A covered channel for cables and propellant lines along the tank wall.
parts.detail: You cannot run a cable through a tank of liquid oxygen. The wiring tunnel is the long cover on the outside of every big tank: inside it run the control cables, the pressurisation lines and the feed line from the upper tank to the engine. Protected cables are cables that keep working: reliability +1 %.
parts.real: Delta II / Saturn V systems tunnel

parts.name: Helium pressurant sphere
parts.desc: High-pressure helium that keeps the tanks full of pressure as they drain.
parts.role: A pressure bottle that pushes gas into the tanks as propellant leaves.
parts.detail: As an engine drinks from a tank, something must take the propellant's place or the tank would collapse and the pump would cavitate. Helium at 300 bar from this sphere does it: it is the lightest gas that does not freeze in liquid oxygen. The composite-overwrapped bottle (a thin liner wound in carbon fibre) is the state of the art, and the thing that failed on the AMOS-6 pad explosion. Reliability +0.6 %.
cons: 300 bar of stored energy next to the tank
parts.real: Delta II second-stage helium spheres, Falcon 9 COPVs

parts.name: Nitrogen cold-gas sphere
parts.desc: Cold nitrogen puffs to turn the ship. Simple, weak.
parts.role: A nitrogen bottle feeding small cold-gas thrusters.
parts.detail: The simplest attitude control there is: a bottle of nitrogen and a few valves. No combustion, nothing to ignite, almost nothing to go wrong. The puffs are weak (Isp about 70 s), so it turns the ship slowly and runs out sooner than a proper thruster pack.
cons: Slow to turn a heavy ship
parts.real: Delta II second-stage nitrogen sphere, Falcon 9 cold-gas RCS

parts.name: RCS thruster pack
parts.desc: Small thrusters to turn the ship in space.
parts.role: Small thrusters that turn the ship in space.
parts.detail: A reaction control pack: a cluster of tiny thrusters that fire sideways to roll, pitch and yaw the ship where there is no air for fins to bite. Needed to point the ship for burns and entry.

parts.name: Engine gimbal
parts.desc: Lets the engine swivel to steer during the burn.
parts.role: Lets the main engine swivel to steer during a burn.
parts.detail: A gimbal ring lets the engine tilt a few degrees, so the thrust itself steers the ship while it burns. This is how real rockets fly straight without big fins.
cons: Only works while the engine burns

parts.name: Reaction wheel
parts.desc: Spins a flywheel to turn without fuel. Slow.
parts.role: Spins a flywheel to turn without fuel. Slow.
parts.detail: A spinning wheel inside the ship: speed it up and the ship turns the other way, no propellant needed. Slow and gentle; good for pointing an antenna, not for a landing.

parts.name: Star tracker
parts.desc: A camera that reads the stars to know which way the ship points.
parts.role: A camera that finds the ship's attitude from the star field.
parts.detail: Gyroscopes drift. A star tracker photographs the sky, matches the pattern against a catalogue of thousands of stars, and tells the computer exactly which way the ship points, to a few arcseconds. Without one the dish and the burns are pointed by dead reckoning. Reliability +0.5 %.
pros: Exact pointing for burns and the dish

parts.name: Ablative heat shield
parts.desc: Chars away to carry the heat off. Heavy and dependable.
parts.role: An ablative shield that chars away to carry heat off.
parts.detail: The ablative heat shield burns slowly and deliberately during entry, carrying the heat away with the charred material. Heavy, dependable, and the only thing between the crew and plasma.

parts.name: Ablative heat shield, large
parts.desc: A wider shield: more drag in thin Martian air.
parts.role: A wide ablative shield: slows the ship harder in thin air.
parts.detail: Mars has so little air that a wider shield matters: more area means more drag and a gentler, cooler entry. This one fits a large stack.

parts.name: Ceramic tiles
parts.desc: Half the mass. Chips if anything hits it on the way up.
parts.role: Ceramic tiles: half the mass, chips if struck.
parts.detail: Ceramic tiles insulate instead of burning away, so they weigh half as much. They are brittle: a piece of ice or foam on ascent can crack them, and a cracked tile on entry is how Columbia was lost.

parts.name: Inflatable heat shield
parts.desc: A stack of inflatable rings under a woven ceramic cloth. Huge area, new technology.
parts.role: An inflatable aeroshell: the widest shield for the least mass.
parts.detail: Packed small for launch, inflated to a wide cone before entry: stacked rings of woven fabric under a blanket of silicon-carbide cloth. The biggest drag area of any shield, which is exactly what thin Martian air needs. It has flown once, from orbit, in 2022, so reliability is lower.

parts.name: Radiator panel
parts.desc: Dumps cabin heat into space; vacuum is a thermos.
parts.role: Dumps cabin heat into space.
parts.detail: Vacuum is a thermos: nothing conducts heat away. A radiator panel sheds the heat from electronics and people by glowing it off into space.

parts.name: MLI insulation blanket
parts.desc: Twenty layers of gold foil: keeps the cold in and the Sun out.
parts.role: Multilayer insulation: the gold foil on every spacecraft.
parts.detail: Multilayer insulation is 10 to 20 sheets of aluminised plastic with nothing between them. In vacuum, heat can only cross by radiation, and every shiny layer bounces most of it back. It keeps cryogenic propellant cold and electronics warm. Reliability +0.3 %.
pros: Keeps propellant cold and electronics warm
cons: Useless in air: only works in vacuum

parts.name: Landing legs ×4
parts.desc: Four legs. Touch down below 3 m/s.
parts.role: Four landing legs. Touch down below 3 m/s.
parts.detail: Four shock-absorbing legs with pads. They clamp around the engine so the feet reach the ground. A touchdown faster than about 3 m/s, or leaning more than 20 degrees, breaks them.

parts.name: Heavy landing legs ×4
parts.desc: Longer legs with a wider stance for a tall, heavy ship.
parts.role: Long legs with a wide stance: a tall ship stays upright on a slope.
parts.detail: A tall ship on a slope tips over on short legs. These reach further out and crush more honeycomb on touchdown, so a heavier ship can land a little harder and on rougher ground.
pros: Wide stance for a tall ship

parts.name: Supersonic parachute
parts.desc: Opens at Mach 1.7 in the thin Martian air.
parts.role: A supersonic parachute for the thin Martian air.
parts.detail: Mars has so little air that the chute opens at Mach 1.7 and still cannot slow the ship enough by itself. It buys time and speed before the engines light for the last kilometres.

parts.name: Drogue chute
parts.desc: A small, strong chute that opens first and steadies the ship.
parts.role: A small chute that opens early, stops the tumbling and slows the ship a little.
parts.detail: A drogue is small and tough: it can open faster and higher than a main chute, stop the capsule tumbling, and pull the main chute out. Alone it slows the ship only a little; with a main chute it makes the whole descent gentler.

parts.name: Splash floats
parts.desc: Keeps the capsule upright after the splashdown home.
parts.role: Keeps the capsule upright after splashdown.
parts.detail: Inflatable floats for the return to Earth: they keep the capsule the right way up in the sea until the ship arrives.
pros: Keeps the capsule upright at sea
cons: Only matters on the way home

parts.name: Landing airbags
parts.desc: Bounce instead of landing. Pathfinder did it; a heavy ship cannot.
parts.role: A cocoon of airbags: the ship bounces to a stop instead of landing on legs.
parts.detail: Pathfinder and the Mars rovers hit the ground inside a ball of airbags and bounced for a kilometre. It works for a light lander and is cheaper than legs, but a crewed ship is heavy and the crew will not enjoy the bounces: reliability 97.5 %.

parts.name: Spare O₂ tank
parts.desc: One EVA refill. A person breathes about 0.84 kg of O₂ a day.
parts.role: One spare EVA oxygen refill.
parts.detail: A high-pressure bottle of oxygen for the suit. A person breathes about 0.84 kg of oxygen a day; one bottle is one refill at the ship between walks outside.

parts.name: Oxygen tank, double
parts.desc: Two refills in one tank.
parts.role: Two EVA refills in one tank.
parts.detail: One tank, twice the oxygen: two refills for the suit. A little lighter than two separate bottles, because one valve and one mounting serve both.

parts.name: CO₂ scrubber
parts.desc: Keeps the cabin air breathable for months.
parts.role: Removes the CO₂ the crew breathes out.
parts.detail: Without a scrubber the cabin fills with carbon dioxide in days. This one keeps the air breathable for months, the way the scrubbers on Apollo 13 did once the crew improvised a fix.

parts.name: Radiation shelter
parts.desc: Water-walled corner to hide in during a solar storm.
parts.role: A water-walled corner to hide in during a solar storm.
parts.detail: Between the planets there is no magnetic field to hide behind. When the Sun throws a storm, the crew climbs into this shelter, whose walls are tanks of water, until it passes.

parts.name: Water recycler
parts.desc: Recovers about 98 % of the water, like the ISS.
parts.role: Recovers about 98 % of the water.
parts.detail: Turns yesterday's water back into today's. The ISS recovers about 98 %; without it a long trip would need tonnes of water.

parts.name: Solar panel
parts.desc: 2 kW at Earth, about 43 % of that at Mars.
parts.role: Two kilowatts at Earth, less than half that at Mars.
parts.detail: Solar panels power the scanners, the radios and the life support. Mars is farther from the Sun, so the same panel makes only about 43 % of the power it makes at Earth.

parts.name: Solar wing, large
parts.desc: 5 kW at Earth. A deployable wing, folded for launch.
parts.role: A deployable wing: five kilowatts at Earth.
parts.detail: A folded wing of triple-junction cells that unfurls in orbit. Five kilowatts at Earth, about two at Mars: enough to run everything and charge the batteries for the night.

parts.name: Battery
parts.desc: Stores power for the night.
parts.role: Stores power for the night.
parts.detail: A battery pack that carries the ship through the night and through burns when the panels point away from the Sun.

parts.name: Radioisotope generator (RTG)
parts.desc: 300 W from decaying plutonium: day, night, dust storm, anywhere.
parts.role: A nuclear battery: a small, steady trickle of power that never depends on the Sun.
parts.detail: A few kilograms of plutonium-238 glow red-hot for decades; thermocouples turn the heat into about 300 W. No Sun needed, so it works through the night, through dust storms, and at the same strength at Mars as at Earth. Curiosity and Perseverance run on one. Very expensive and politically hard to launch.
pros: Same power at Mars, at night, in dust
Most reliable part in the hangar

parts.name: Fuel cell
parts.desc: 2.5 kW from hydrogen and oxygen, and drinking water as a by-product.
parts.role: Burns hydrogen and oxygen quietly into electricity and drinking water.
parts.detail: Apollo and the Shuttle ran on fuel cells: hydrogen and oxygen combine across a membrane to make electricity, heat and pure water the crew drinks. Strong power without panels, but the reactants run out in weeks, not months.
parts.real: Shuttle PRSD fuel cells, 7 kW each

parts.name: Low-gain antenna
parts.desc: Slow but it works from anywhere.
parts.role: Slow but works from anywhere.
parts.detail: A low-gain antenna: no pointing needed, a trickle of data in any direction. Enough for voice, telemetry and small files. Without any antenna nothing you find can be sent home.

parts.name: Medium-gain horn
parts.desc: A horn: faster than the omni, forgiving of pointing errors.
parts.role: A horn antenna: a useful middle between the omni and the dish.
parts.detail: A horn concentrates the signal into a wide cone. It needs only rough pointing, so it keeps working while the ship manoeuvres, and it sends data many times faster than the low-gain stick.

parts.name: High-gain dish
parts.desc: Uploads science fast. Must be pointed.
parts.role: Uploads science fast. Must be pointed.
parts.detail: A high-gain dish sends data hundreds of times faster, but only when it points at Earth. The science of the mission goes home through this.

parts.name: Relay smallsat
parts.desc: A small satellite left in Mars orbit to relay data home.
parts.role: A relay satellite released into Mars orbit: a dish in the sky even when Earth is below the horizon.
parts.detail: Every Mars rover talks to Earth through orbiters overhead. This smallsat rides on the side of the ship, is released into orbit, and relays data from the surface with its own dish and solar panels, so the crew can send science home even when Earth has set.
pros: Fast uploads from the surface, any time of day

parts.name: Armor plating
parts.desc: Absorbs one small debris hit.
parts.role: Absorbs one small debris hit.
parts.detail: A sheet of layered shielding like the ISS carries. A small piece of orbital debris hits it instead of the tank. Good for one hit.

parts.name: Whipple shield
parts.desc: A thin bumper plate that shatters debris before it reaches the wall.
parts.role: A thin outer bumper that turns a debris strike into harmless spray.
parts.detail: Fred Whipple's 1947 idea: put a thin sheet a hand's width in front of the wall. A hypervelocity particle hits the sheet and vaporises into a cloud that spreads out before it reaches the wall. Half the mass of solid armour for the same protection.

parts.name: Spectrometer
parts.desc: Reads what a rock is made of.
parts.role: Reads what a rock is made of.
parts.detail: Fires a laser at a rock and reads the colours of the spark: every element has its own signature. This is how Perseverance tells basalt from clay from hematite.

parts.name: Ground radar
parts.desc: Finds buried ice for the return fuel.
parts.role: Finds buried ice for the return fuel.
parts.detail: A ground-penetrating radar that sees metres into the soil. Buried ice is water, and water plus the Martian air is methane and oxygen: the return trip.
pros: Finds buried ice for return fuel

parts.name: Core drill
parts.desc: Sealed sample tubes, like Perseverance.
parts.role: Sealed sample tubes, like Perseverance.
parts.detail: A core drill that cuts a finger-sized sample and seals it in a tube. Sealed samples are the only ones that count when you get home.

parts.name: Science camera
parts.desc: Stereo and infrared cameras: the geologist's eyes.
parts.role: Stereo and infrared cameras for mapping the site and choosing rocks.
parts.detail: A pair of colour cameras for stereo distance and an infrared camera that sees minerals by their heat signature. The maps the crew makes on the surface start here.

parts.name: Weather station
parts.desc: Wind, pressure, dust and temperature, every minute.
parts.role: Measures wind, pressure, dust and temperature on the surface.
parts.detail: Booms with wind, temperature, pressure, humidity and dust sensors. Dust storms are what kill solar-powered missions; knowing one is coming is worth the twenty kilograms.

parts.name: Seismometer
parts.desc: Listens to marsquakes to see inside the planet.
parts.role: Listens to marsquakes: the only way to see the inside of the planet.
parts.detail: Set on the ground under a wind shield, it feels quakes smaller than a footstep. From the echoes, scientists measured the size of the Martian core for the first time.
pros: Sees the inside of the planet
cons: Must be placed by hand, away from the ship

parts.name: Sample containers
parts.desc: Sealed tubes for three samples. Every kilogram costs return Δv.
parts.role: Sealed tubes for three samples.
parts.detail: Storage for three sealed samples in the ship. Every kilogram you bring back is a kilogram the return burn has to lift: choose your rocks.

parts.name: Sample vault
parts.desc: A sealed vault for six samples.
parts.role: A sealed, temperature-controlled vault for six samples.
parts.detail: Six tubes in a vault that keeps them cold and sealed all the way home, so the chemistry inside is what it was on Mars.
parts.real: Mars Sample Return orbiting sample container

parts.name: Cheap seals (−$100k)
parts.desc: Saves money. Not rated below 5 °C.
parts.role: Saves $100k. Not rated below 5 °C.
parts.detail: Cheaper seals for the tank joints. They work fine on a warm pad. In the cold they stiffen and leak hot gas: the Challenger booster seal did exactly this at 2 °C, after engineers had warned against the launch.
